Period schedule:

Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

repairs.reason: register backfill (founder ruling 2026-08-02; testing.md C3 / ARV-D-011..013, ARV-D-026)

edits.note: the first of the two completion hits. U10 of a p10 compact is its LAST unit but carries no synthesis licence. The five strands are NAMED in the same sentence and all survive; what goes is the claim that a chapter was worked through, which is false whenever this plan is a teacher's first exposure

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading Badal and Moti Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to look at the title and the chapter illustration. Ask: What do you think this story is about? Who might Badal and Moti be?

Teacher reads the full prose text of Badal and Moti (pp.15–17) aloud with expression, pausing at key moments — Badal finding the puppy, the naming scene, and the rescue. Students follow in their textbooks.
Teacher reads the text a second time, inviting students to read along softly (choral read-along). Pause after each paragraph to ask a quick oral check: 'What happened just now?'
Students share in one sentence what they found most surprising or touching about the story. Teacher collects a few responses without evaluation, building curiosity for the next sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: This is students' first encounter with the prose text; keep the mood warm and story-like, not quiz-like. Let the rescue scene land with drama — slow down and read Moti's barking and the rope moment with deliberate pacing. Students who find the text long will stay engaged if the teacher performs rather than recites.
materials: Chalk/whiteboard to write character names Badal and Moti

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: What Happened and Why

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.18): answer factual questions 1–4 about the story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher does a quick paired re-read: pairs take turns reading one paragraph each from the story (pp.15–17) to warm up and settle into the text.

Teacher asks questions 1–4 from Let us think — A (p.18) orally, one at a time. Students discuss in pairs for a moment, then one student shares the answer. Teacher revoices, corrects gently, and writes key answers on the board.

Teacher reads the five True/False statements from Let us think — A (p.18) aloud. Students hold up a thumb-up for True and thumb-down for False. After each, teacher asks 'How do you know?' and a student finds the evidence in the text.
Students write their answers to questions 1–4 in their notebooks independently. Teacher circulates and gives brief feedback on sentence formation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the full story read aloud, students now work with specific textual evidence. A common error is confusing 'Moti caught Badal's scent' with 'Moti caught Badal's photo' — the True/False item directly addresses this; use it as a moment to discuss how dogs use smell, not sight, to track. Keep the oral discussion warm and inviting before moving to written answers.

periods.activity_title: Pair Talk: Pets, Falls, and Personal Experiences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.19): pair discussion on falling, pets, and ideal pet choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the story moment where Badal falls into the pit and says: 'Has anything like this ever happened to you — or do you know someone with a pet like Moti?' This sets up the pair talk.

Pairs discuss Let us think — B, question 1 (p.19): a time they fell down — how it happened, who helped. Teacher circulates and prompts students who go quiet: 'Tell your partner where you were when you fell.'

Pairs discuss questions 2 and 3 from Let us think — B (p.19): whether they have a pet, and which animal they would choose as a pet and why. Teacher listens and notes interesting or unusual pet choices for whole-class sharing.
Whole-class share-out: four or five students share their ideal pet choice and one reason. Teacher invites brief questions from classmates ('Why a parrot and not a dog?').

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not personally fallen or do not have a pet can still speak meaningfully — they may know a friend or neighbour with a pet, or can imagine. Redirect shy students gently: 'You can tell us about an animal you have seen or liked.' The goal is fluent personal narration, not a correct answer.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Sequence: Story Events in Order

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — A (p.20): number story events in sequence after listening to the story read aloud.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the activity: 'I will read the story aloud. Listen carefully — after I finish, you will put six story events in the right order in your textbook (p.20).' Preview the six sentences on the board so students know what to listen for.
Teacher reads the transcript (pp.15–17) aloud at a measured pace, the first time through. Students listen with textbooks closed.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time. Students may now look at the six sentences in their textbook (p.20) and begin forming an idea of the order.
Teacher reads the transcript a third time, slowly. Students write their sequence numbers in the boxes on p.20.

Pairs compare their sequences and discuss any differences. Teacher then works through the correct order (1-Badal finds the puppy, 2-They name him Moti, 3-Badal falls into the pit, 4-Moti joins the search, 5-Moti barks at the pit, 6-Badal hugs Moti) on the board, asking students to explain each placement.
Students retell the story to their partner in the correct order using only the six sentences as a scaffold. Teacher listens and affirms confident retellings.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequencing task develops careful listening and narrative comprehension together. Read expressively and at a pace that allows the crisis moment — the muddy lane and the pit — to register clearly, since that is the pivot around which students sort the later events. Students who struggle with written sequencing can whisper the order to a partner first.
materials: Chalk/whiteboard for displaying the six sentences

periods.activity_title: Daily Routine Talk: Before, During, and After School

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — A (p.21): pair talk on daily routine before, during, and after school.
Let us speak — B (p.21): complete and say aloud the daily-routine sentence frame.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens: 'Badal went to school every day. What about you — what does your day look like?' Brief whole-class warm-up where two or three students name one thing they do in the morning before school.

Pairs take turns using Let us speak — A (p.21) to describe their day in three parts: before school, during school, and after going home. Each partner speaks for a sustained turn; the listener asks one follow-up question.

Teacher writes the sentence frame from Let us speak — B (p.21) on the board. Students complete the blanks aloud with their partner ('Every day I ___ up at ___ in the morning…'). Teacher circulates, helping students fill in natural details.

Four or five volunteers share their full three-part daily routine with the class using the completed sentence frame as a scaffold. Classmates listen and note one thing that is similar to and one thing different from their own day.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence frame in Let us speak — B is a scaffold, not a script — encourage students to personalise the blanks rather than copy a neighbour's choices. Students who wake very early or have non-standard routines should feel their reality is welcome; the frame bends to fit real lives. Keep the sharing phase lively by asking the audience brief comparison questions.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.19): add '-ed' to walk, play, talk, ask, touch.
Let us learn — B (p.20): match word pairs (bat–ball, needle–thread, etc.).

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'lived', 'loved', 'played', 'gathered', 'thanked' on the board — all from the story. Ask: 'What do you notice about how each word ends?' Guide students to see the '-ed' pattern and connect it to actions that have already happened.

Teacher models: 'walk + ed = walked' on the board, saying both forms aloud. Students work through Let us learn — A (p.19) — adding '-ed' to walk, play, talk, ask, touch — first orally as a class, then written individually in notebooks.
Teacher introduces Let us learn — B (p.20): 'Some words always go together — like bat and ball. Can you think of others?' Pairs brainstorm briefly, then open textbooks to the matching task.

Students complete the word-pair matching in their textbooks (p.20), using crayons or pencils to colour each pair the same colour as instructed. Teacher circulates and checks pairs: paper–pencil, chair–table, lock–key, idli–sambar, bat–ball, needle–thread.
Quick oral check: teacher calls a word and students call the pair. 'Bat!' → 'Ball!' 'Idli!' → 'Sambar!' End on a lively note.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-ed' words all appear in the story, so students have already met them in context — use that familiarity to make the grammar feel like a discovery rather than a new rule. A common error is writing 'plaied' for 'played'; since 'play' ends in a consonant-vowel pattern, the '-ed' simply attaches. The word-pair task builds vocabulary through association and works well as a game; keep the pace brisk.

periods.activity_title: Ordering a Picture Story: The Pigeon and the Ant

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.21): number six jumbled pictures of the pigeon-and-ant story in correct order.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the activity: 'We have been reading about how Moti saved Badal. Now we meet another pair of friends — a pigeon and an ant — who help each other. Look at the six pictures on p.21.' Students spend a moment looking at each picture quietly.

Teacher guides a whole-class picture walk through the six images on p.21, asking: 'What is happening here? Who is in trouble? What does the pigeon do? What does the ant do later?' Students observe and respond orally.

Pairs discuss the logical order of the six pictures. What must have happened first? What comes just before the ant bites the hunter's hand? Students then number the pictures individually in their textbooks (p.21).

Teacher reveals and explains the correct sequence: ant falls into stream → pigeon drops a leaf → ant climbs onto leaf and is safe → hunter aims at pigeon → ant bites hunter's hand → pigeon flies away safely. Students check and correct their own numbering.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture-ordering task builds narrative logic — the ability to read visual cause-and-effect — which is the key skill here. Students may debate the order of the hunter and the rescue scenes; use that productive disagreement to ask 'What clue in the picture tells you which comes first?' The story of the pigeon and ant echoes the friendship theme of Badal and Moti, which can be noted briefly to reinforce the chapter's central idea.

periods.activity_title: Fill the Story and Add Punctuation Marks

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.22): fill in blanks using the word box to complete the pigeon-and-ant story.
Let us write — C (p.22): add '?' or '.' to six sentences using story examples as models.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the word box for Let us write — B (p.22) aloud: leaf, flew, branch, climbed, fell, stream, hunter. Students repeat each word. Teacher checks that all understand 'branch' and 'stream' by pointing to context in the pictures they ordered.

Teacher models the first blank together: 'A dove was resting on a ___ of a tree near a ___.' Students suggest 'branch' and 'stream'; teacher confirms and writes them. Students then complete the remaining blanks individually in their textbooks (p.22). Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck by asking 'What did the ant do when it fell?'

Teacher introduces Let us write — C (p.22), using the two dialogue lines from the chapter ('Can this puppy stay with us, Maa?' and 'Yes beta, but only if you promise…') to show when a question mark versus a full stop is used. Students discuss: 'Is this sentence asking something, or telling something?'

Students complete the six sentences in Let us write — C (p.22) independently, adding '?' or '.'. Teacher reviews answers together orally at the end and asks students to read each completed sentence aloud with appropriate intonation.

periods.teacher_notes: The guided fill-in for Let us write — B builds sentence-level reading comprehension alongside vocabulary use — insist students read the whole sentence before guessing the blank, not just look for a grammatically fitting word. For Let us write — C, connect the question-mark rule to the pupils' own speaking: when their voice goes up at the end of a sentence, it is usually a question. Students often add a question mark to polite requests — 'May I borrow your English textbook' is a good example to discuss.
materials: Chalk/whiteboard for the word box and model sentences

periods.activity_title: Extend the Picture: Children at Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.24): add to the outdoor-play illustration using crayons or colour pencils.

time_bands.activity: Teacher directs students to the illustration on p.24 showing three children playing outdoors — one with a hoop, one with a ball, one on a swing. Ask: 'What games do you play with your friends? Could any of those fit into this picture?'
Students discuss in pairs what they would like to add to the picture — another child, a pet like Moti, a tree, a kite, a different game. Each pair shares one idea aloud before drawing begins.

Students use crayons or colour pencils to add their chosen elements to the picture on p.24. Teacher circulates, asking individuals to describe what they are drawing and why they chose it: 'Why did you add a dog?' 'Where is your new friend playing?'

Students share their completed pictures with a neighbour and say in one or two sentences what they added and why. Teacher selects three or four students to show and describe their picture to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The illustration activity is genuinely open — there is no single correct addition. Encourage students who draw a puppy to connect it to Moti and the chapter's theme of friendship; this makes the creative act feel anchored rather than arbitrary. Students who finish early can label the elements they drew, practising the writing skills built earlier in the chapter.

periods.activity_title: Closing Unit: Revisiting the Story of Badal and Moti

time_bands.activity: Students do a paired repeated reading of any page from Badal and Moti (pp.15–17) they choose. One partner reads, the other listens and then retells the page's events in two sentences.

Whole-class oral retelling: teacher points to moments from the story — the cold evening, the naming scene, the rainy day, the rescue — and invites different students to narrate each moment in their own words, building a spoken version of the whole story together.

Quick word-work game: teacher calls out a base verb from the chapter (live, play, gather, thank, love) and students race to say the '-ed' form and use it in a sentence. Then teacher calls a word (bat, needle, lock, idli) and students call its pair.

Students look back at their written answers to the comprehension questions and their fill-in story and choose one sentence they want to improve. Teacher models how to make one sentence more precise or more vivid, then students revise their chosen sentence.

Students observe the picture they extended on p.24 and in two sentences write what their addition tells about friendship or play. Two or three students share their sentences aloud, and the class discusses: 'How is your picture connected to what Badal and Moti teaches us?'

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws together the reading, speaking, word work, writing, and creative work — connecting them through the central themes of friendship, loyalty, and care. Use the retelling phase to assess fluency and story comprehension informally, noting students who can sequence events confidently versus those who still need the six-sentence scaffold. The sentence-revision moment is brief but meaningful: it builds the habit of re-reading and improving one's own writing.

items.source_context: Village boy Badal, stray puppy Moti, rescue from a pit, loyalty and friendship.
items.item_stem: On a rainy day, Badal slipped on a muddy lane. What happened to him after he slipped?

options.label: A
options.text: He climbed a tree to stay safe.

options.label: B
options.text: He fell into a deep pit.

options.label: C
options.text: He found Moti waiting for him.

options.label: D
options.text: He ran home to his mother.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student remembers Badal's mother but confuses her role — Badal could not go home because he was trapped.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reflects a scrambled understanding of the rescue sequence — Moti arrived later, after the fall.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows the student may have confused the pit scene with the pigeon-and-ant story's tree setting.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves explicit information and judges statement accuracy using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Village boy Badal, stray puppy Moti, rescue from a pit, loyalty and friendship.
items.item_stem: Badal's mother agreed to let the puppy stay only because Badal was cold and lonely. Read the story carefully and say whether this is true or false, and write one sentence from the story that supports your answer.

options.text: Badal's mother agreed to let the puppy stay only because Badal was cold and lonely.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: False. Badal's mother agreed to let the puppy stay only if Badal promised to take care of it — her condition was about responsibility, not loneliness.

items.item_stem:
Listen to the teacher read the story of Badal and Moti aloud. Then look at the four events below and mark them 1 to 4 in the order they happened in the story.
— Moti followed Badal's scent and barked near the pit.
— Badal found a shivering puppy by the side of the road.
— Badal's mother gathered the neighbours to search for him.
— Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.

options.text: Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti happens second.
Badal found a shivering puppy by the side of the road happens first.
Badal's mother gathered the neighbours happens third.
Moti followed Badal's scent and barked near the pit happens fourth.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Correct sequence: 1 — Badal finds the puppy; 2 — Badal and his mother name him Moti; 3 — Badal's mother gathers the neighbours; 4 — Moti follows the scent and barks near the pit.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a story read aloud, sequences events, and narrates personal experiences using a prose narrative as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Moti became Badal's best friend by always being with him — eating, playing, and going everywhere together. Tell your partner about a friend, a family member, or a pet who is always there for you. Say at least two things this person or animal does that shows they care about you.

expected_elements: Names the friend, family member, or pet clearly.
Gives at least two specific caring actions.
Speaks in complete sentences with audible voice.

items.source_context: Pigeon-and-ant friendship story, word-box fill-in, question mark versus full stop punctuation.
items.item_stem:
Read the four sentences below. They tell the story of the pigeon and the ant, but they are in the wrong order. Write the numbers 1 to 4 in the boxes to show the correct order.
□ The ant bit the hunter's hand so the pigeon could fly away safely.
□ A dove was resting on a branch near a stream when an ant fell in.
□ A hunter aimed at the dove, and the ant saw him.
□ The dove dropped a leaf into the stream and the ant climbed on it to safety.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1–2–4–3 (correct order: dove on branch, ant falls in → dove drops leaf, ant is safe → hunter aims at dove → ant bites hunter, dove flies away).

answer_key.left: A dove was resting on a branch near a stream when an ant fell in.
The dove dropped a leaf into the stream and the ant climbed on it to safety.
A hunter aimed at the dove, and the ant saw him.
The ant bit the hunter's hand so the pigeon could fly away safely.

items.item_stem: The pigeon and the ant helped each other when they were in danger — just like Moti helped Badal. Write two or three sentences about a time you helped a friend, or a time a friend helped you. Use a full stop at the end of each sentence.

expected_elements: Names who helped and the situation briefly.
Describes the helping action in one sentence.
Ends each sentence with a full stop.

items.source_context: Past-tense '-ed' verbs from the story; common word pairs (bat–ball, needle–thread, idli–sambar, etc.).
items.item_stem: Choose the correctly formed past-tense word to complete each sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Badal's mother ___ the neighbours to search for him. (gather / gatherred / gathered / gatherd)

items.visual_stimulus:
| Sentence | Choose the correct word |
|---|---|
| Badal's mother ___ the neighbours to search for him. | gather / gatherred / gathered / gatherd |

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing the base form 'gather' shows the student has not yet connected past-tense action to the '-ed' ending.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Doubling the 'r' before '-ed' is a spelling error — the rule of doubling applies only to short-vowel single-consonant endings, not here.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Dropping the final 'e' before adding 'd' shows confusion about when to drop versus simply attach '-ed'.

items.item_stem: Say aloud two past-tense sentences of your own using action words from the story of Badal and Moti. Each sentence must use a different '-ed' word and must describe something a character in the story did.

expected_elements: Uses two different '-ed' verbs from the story.
Each sentence names a story character correctly.
Speaks clearly so '-ed' ending is audible.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 24 showing three children playing outdoors. Match each description on the left with the correct child's activity shown in the picture on the right.
items.visual_stimulus:
| What the child is doing | Activity in the picture |
|---|---|
| Rolling a circular toy along the ground | Hoop rolling |
| Sitting on a hanging seat and swinging | Tree swing |
| Throwing and catching a round object | Tossing a ball |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rolling a circular toy — hoop rolling; sitting on a hanging seat and swinging — tree swing; throwing and catching a round object — tossing a ball.

Sitting on a hanging seat and swinging
Throwing and catching a round object
